qs.q: A public health surveillance team monitors a novel influenza strain that has emerged in Southeast Asia, causing widespread pandemic disease through major genomic segment exchange. Which virological phenomenon describes this genetic alteration?
o: Recombination via template switching during negative-strand synthesis
Antigenic drift driven by point mutations in viral polymerase enzymes
Phenotypic mixing resulting from simultaneous coinfection of a single cell
Complementation occurring between defective viral particles in vivo
Antigenic shift involving the reassortment of segmented RNA genomes
qs.e: Antigenic shift occurs via segment reassortment, typically in coinfected animal hosts, creating novel pandemic strains.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - October 30,

qs.q: A 52-year-old man who had an elective total hip replacement 70 days ago presents with a deep abscess found on imaging involving the joint space. What is the maximum timeframe for SSI surveillance in this patient with an implant?
o: Within 30 days of the index procedure
Within 60 days of the index procedure
Within 90 days of the index procedure
Within 120 days of the index procedure
qs.e: For surgeries involving an implant, such as orthopaedic and spinal surgery, the surveillance window for surgical site infections is extended to 90 days. The standard window for procedures without implants is 30 days.
qs.s: Surgical Site Infections: Types, Risk Factors, Wound Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man receiving total parenteral nutrition is scheduled for weekly laboratory surveillance. Which set of investigations is appropriate to perform on a weekly basis?
o: Catheter site inspection and pulse rate
qs.e: Liver function tests and triglycerides are monitored weekly during TPN therapy, whereas glucose and fluid balance are checked daily or more frequently. Catheter inspection and temperature charting are also performed more often than weekly.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

qs.q: A 68‑year‑old woman is undergoing surveillance after curative colorectal cancer surgery. How often should cross‑sectional liver imaging be performed during the first three years of follow‑up?
qs.e: Annual liver imaging (CT or ultrasound) for three years is recommended to detect hepatic metastases early. More frequent imaging (every 3–6 months) exceeds standard surveillance recommendations.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old man with a 12-year history of extensive ulcerative colitis is scheduled for long-term malignancy surveillance. Which specialized endoscopic technique is recommended during his colonoscopy to detect dysplasia?
qs.e: Chromoendoscopy is specifically recommended during surveillance colonoscopy for dysplasia in patients with long-standing extensive colitis. Capsule endoscopy is primarily used for small bowel Crohn's disease and is not the standard for colonic dysplasia surveillance.
qs.s: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's Disease: MCQs

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with high-risk bladder cancer is undergoing post-treatment surveillance after initial management. According to the protocol, what is the frequency of cystoscopy for high-risk patients during the first two years?
qs.e: High-risk surveillance involves cystoscopy every 3 months for 2 years, then 6-monthly, then yearly. Low-risk surveillance has longer initial intervals starting at 3 months, 12 months, then yearly.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer: Haematuria, TURBT, BCG and Cystectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man undergoes surveillance cystoscopy following successful treatment for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Why is lifelong follow-up mandatory even if initial tumours are cleared?
o: The recurrence rate is near total
Bladder cancer is a field change disease
qs.e: Bladder cancer is a 'field change' disease, meaning the entire urothelial lining is exposed to carcinogens and remains at risk for new tumour formation. Low-risk recurrence is high, but the conceptual reason for lifelong follow-up is the field change phenomenon.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer: Haematuria, TURBT, BCG and Cystectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 64-year-old man with a low-risk localised prostate cancer chooses active surveillance. Which of the following follow-up protocols best aligns with standard management for his condition?
o: PSA every 6 months, DRE every 6 months, immediate repeat biopsy.
PSA every 3–6 months, DRE yearly, repeat MRI and biopsy.
PSA every 3–6 months, DRE yearly, stop surveillance after 2 years.
PSA yearly, DRE every 3 months, routine annual bone scan.
qs.e: Active surveillance for low-risk disease involves monitoring with PSA every 3 to 6 months, annual DRE, and repeat MRI and biopsy, treating only if progression occurs. Routine bone scans are not part of low-risk active surveillance follow-up.
qs.s: Prostate Cancer: Screening, Diagnosis, Staging and Treatment: MCQs

es.q: Discuss the spectrum of gestational trophoblastic disease, focusing on the pathology, clinical features, diagnostic workup, management, surveillance, and specific characteristics of choriocarcinoma and gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
es.m:
- **Definition and Spectrum**: GTD is abnormal proliferation of trophoblast, spanning benign complete and partial hydatidiform moles, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.
- **Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN)**: Invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour form GTN and are very chemosensitive.
- **Complete Mole Features**: Karyotype is 46,XX (all paternal), no foetus, all villi swollen, very high hCG, and 15-20% malignant potential for persistent disease.
- **Partial Mole Features**: Triploid (69,XXY) with one maternal and two paternal sets, foetal tissue
es.s: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Hydatidiform Mole and: Essay questions

es.q: Explain the WHO’s Global Technical Strategy for Malaria 2016–2030, including its main objectives and key interventions for prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance.
es.m:
- **Objective 1**: Ensure universal access to malaria prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.
- **Objective 2**: Accelerate efforts toward elimination and attainment of malaria‑free status.
- **Objective 3**: Transform malaria surveillance into a core intervention.
- **Prevention – vector control**: insecticide‑treated mosquito nets (ITNs) and long‑lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) for all at‑risk persons.
- **Prevention – environmental control**: larval source management and reduction of adult mosquito populations.
- **Prevention – chemoprophylaxis**: use of antimalarial drugs for travelers and high‑risk groups.
- **Prevention – vaccination**: ongoing development and deployment of malaria vac

es.q: Outline the schedule and components of growth monitoring and nutrition surveillance for children from birth to 5 years according to the study note.
es.m:
- **Frequency of monitoring:** Monthly in the first year, every 3 months up to 2 years, and then 6-monthly until 5 years.
- **Measurement plotting:** Weigh, measure length or height, head circumference (under 2 years or if abnormal), and MUAC from 6 months, and plot every measurement.
- **Growth interpretation:** Compare each point with WHO growth standard curves and look at the trend rather than a single point; flat/falling curves or crossing two centile lines require investigation.
- **Infant and young child feeding:** Breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then add complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond.
- **Micronutrients and prevention:** Vitamin A supplem
es.s: Evaluation of the Well Child: Surveillance, Screening, Immunisation: Essay quest

ai.title: Paediatric Developmental Surveillance
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Surveillance in children monitors growth and development to detect delays early. It uses scheduled checks of motor, language, vision, hearing and social skills, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: Developmental surveillance is a systematic, ongoing process of observing a child's milestones and comparing them to age‑appropriate norms to identify concerns early.
b: Routine checks at well‑child visits
Use of simple tools (e.g., Ages and Stages Questionnaire) when formal testing unavailable

sections.p: Concerns are categorised as mild, moderate or severe based on the number of domains missed and the degree of delay from expected age.
b: Mild: 1‑2 month lag in one domain
Moderate: >2 month lag or multiple domains
Severe: >6 month lag or regression

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the most common contributors are nutritional deficiency, chronic infection and environmental deprivation.
b: Malnutrition (protein‑energy, micronutrient deficiencies)
Repeated infections (malaria, HIV, TB, chronic otitis media)
Perinatal insults (birth asphyxia, prematurity)
Social factors (poverty, limited stimulation, parental illness)
Rare genetic or metabolic disorders

sections.p: Parents or health workers notice missed milestones, poor eye contact, limited speech, abnormal tone or failure to sit, crawl or walk at expected ages.
b: Delayed sitting by 9 months
No words by 18 months
Persistent head lag after 4 months

sections.p: Investigations are guided by the suspected cause and availability of tests.

t.b: Is growth adequate? Low values suggest malnutrition or chronic disease
Is HIV infection present? Positive result prompts ART and targeted developmental support
Is anaemia contributing? Low haemoglobin supports iron deficiency or chronic infection
Is ocular pathology present? Abnormal reflex suggests cataract or retinopathy
Is hearing loss present? No startle or voice response indicates impairment

b: Regression of previously acquired skills
Seizures or abnormal movements
Persistent fever or failure to thrive despite nutrition
Severe visual or hearing loss

sections.p: Address underlying cause, provide targeted stimulation and monitor progress.
b: Nutritional rehabilitation: therapeutic foods, micronutrient supplementation
Treat infections: antimalarials, antibiotics, ART for HIV, TB therapy
Early intervention: caregiver coaching, play‑based therapy, speech or physiotherapy where available
Vaccination updates (influenza, pneumococcal, measles) to prevent further illness

sections.p: Schedule regular surveillance visits and educate families on stimulating activities.
b: Re‑assess milestones every 3 months for children <2 years, then every 6 months
Promote exclusive breastfeeding, adequate complementary feeding, and safe play environments
Community health worker home visits to reinforce stimulation

sections.p: Developmental surveillance is distinct from disease‑specific screening.
b: Not the same as newborn hearing screening (which is a single test)
Different from growth monitoring alone, which does not assess cognition or motor skills

sections.p: Some findings may appear normal despite underlying problems.
b: Normal weight with micronutrient deficiency can mask cognitive delay
Mild anaemia may not explain severe motor lag, prompting further neuro‑assessment

whenToSeekHelp: Seizures or unexplained loss of consciousness
Severe malnutrition (MUAC <11.5 cm) or failure to thrive

faq.q: What is the first step if a child misses a milestone?
faq.a: Re‑measure growth, review nutrition and infection history, and repeat the surveillance check in 4‑6 weeks.

faq.q: How often should developmental surveillance be performed in the first two years?
faq.a: Every 3 months until age 2, then every 6 months up to school age.

faq.q: Can a child with normal weight still have developmental delay?
faq.a: Yes; weight reflects nutrition but does not assess cognition, language or motor function.

exam: A 14‑month child cannot sit unsupported but has normal weight – what investigations are indicated and why? — Assess vision, hearing, and screen for anaemia; normal weight does not rule out sensory or neurological causes.

During a surveillance visit you note a 4‑month lag in speech in a 2‑year‑old with HIV on ART – what is your next management step? — Intensify speech stimulation, refer to community therapist, and review ART adherence and viral load.

A caregiver reports that the child has stopped crawling after previously achieving it – which red flag does this represent and what urgent action is required? — Regression is a red flag; arrange immediate referral for neuro‑imaging and specialist assessment.
In a rural clinic without audiometers, how would you screen for hearing loss during surveillance? — Use behavioural response to a spoon tap or whispered voice; absent response warrants referral.

A child with severe malnutrition shows normal developmental milestones after 2 weeks of therapeutic feeding – how should you interpret this? — Rapid nutritional improvement can mask underlying delay; continue surveillance and consider neuro‑developmental testing.

What distinguishes developmental surveillance from growth monitoring in low‑resource settings? — Surveillance includes motor, language, social and sensory checks, whereas growth monitoring only tracks weight/height.

A 6‑month infant presents with head lag and poor eye contact; what are the most likely causes in an East African setting? — Malnutrition, chronic malaria or HIV infection, and perinatal hypoxia are top considerations.

Why is it important to vaccinate children before starting biologic therapy for juvenile arthritis? — Vaccination reduces infection risk that could worsen developmental outcomes during immunosuppression.
